title: Test: "Continue with Microsoft" only when your Microsoft account links to GitHub
excerpt: Refs: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/338823 - [ ] windows - [ ] macOS Complexity: 3 --- ## Context Last round (#333246) put **Continue with Microsoft** in sign-in dialogs behind a setting. Turning it on for everyone would show the button to people it can't help, like anyone whose Microsoft account isn't linked to a GitHub account. So now VS Code checks first. The check runs silently in the background. It asks the OS broker for the work and school accounts on your machine, trades each one for a short-lived GitHub token, and asks GitHub who that is. If one of them is linked to a GitHub account (for most of us, an EMU), you get the button. Nothing is saved, and the GitHub token used for the check is revoked. `chat.microsoftAuthentication.enabled` now takes three values: - `auto`: run the check, and offer the button only if it finds a link - `always`: offer the button without checking - `never`: don't offer it, and don't check The button also shows up in a new place: the "Welcome to VS Code" screen a fresh install opens on, as an icon next to Apple. ## Setup Use a work machine where your Microsoft work account is signed in to the OS. Everything here runs in `code-insiders --transient`, which uses throwaway data and extension folders, so you start signed out of everything. ## `auto` Run `code-insiders --transient`. The welcome screen opens with GitHub, Google and Apple. After a short delay, the Microsoft icon should join them. You don't need to change any settings, since Insiders already has `auto`. - How long did it take? Did the icon popping in feel natural or jarring? - Skip the welcome screen and click **Sign In** in the title bar. Is the option in that dialog too? ## `always` Start another `code-insiders --transient` and add this to your settings: ```json "microsoft-authentication.implementation": "msal-no-broker" ``` Click **Reload** when VS Code asks. The Microsoft icon should stay away this time. Now set `"chat.microsoftAuthentication.enabled": "always"`. The icon and the dialog option should come back. ## `never` Set it to `never`. The option should be gone from both the welcome screen and the **Sign In** dialog. ## Then sign in When you're done with the settings, set it back to `auto` or `always`, click **Continue with Microsoft**, and go through sign-in. - The confirmation shows your GitHub handle and nothing else. Is that enough to decide? - Once you're signed in, does Copilot work like it normally does? - Did anything along the way confuse you or feel broken? ## Notes - `auto` depends on the OS broker. Windows on ARM and Linux don't have it yet, so `auto` won't find anything there. - `msal-no-broker` sends Microsoft sign-in through the browser instead of the OS prompt. title: Agent turn should not end while background commands are still running
excerpt: ## Problem In agent mode, a turn can end — and its reply read as "done" — while the chat's **"Waiting for x background commands"** indicator is still live. The count is also opaque: a **crashed** session is indistinguishable from a **slow** one, and over a working day the background-task count only grows, with nothing ever inspected or cleaned up. ## What I see locally (setup + observed facts) - Setup: a local **OpenCode** instance configured as a custom endpoint for GitHub Copilot Chat (OpenCode itself lists the available LLM models). Every fact below is observed with this configuration. - A sync command that exceeds its timeout is moved to the background **silently**. - Session state is known to the runtime (completion is reported, if at all, in the *next* turn) but is not available when the agent finalizes a turn — so a truthful end-of-turn evaluation is hard to produce. - Background sessions **survive window reloads and new chat sessions**, which can neither see nor stop them: a concrete source of the daily accumulation. - Observed today: a test-suite command exceeded its sync timeout and moved to the background; the next turn ended and read as "done" with the indicator still live; and a session whose stdout had gone silent was impossible to distinguish from one still producing results. ## Proposal - End-of-turn rule: every background session started for the task is **finished**, or the agent has **explicitly evaluated** each pending one (keep running / stop / stop and relaunch) and says so in the final reply (which session, why, how to stop it). - Surface session state (running / finished / failed, exit code) to the agent at turn finalization — it is already tracked, just not visible at that moment. - Give the agent those sessions as **one grouped, machine-readable inventory** (single call) — the precondition that makes the evaluation above applicable. - Make the indicator honest and actionable: per-session state, expansion into a list, a stop action per session — stale sessions become stoppable without the agent. - Announce the sync→background switch; report a session's completion and keep its output retrievable, so nothing is lost when a command times out to background. - On chat-session end, offer to stop the sessions it started; leftovers from previous windows stay visible and stoppable. - Optionally a setting for the preferred end-of-turn behavior (wait / evaluate / allow detached). ## Why - **Performance**: fewer follow-up round-trips caused by continuing with steps that depend on results the background sessions had not produced yet. - **Coherence**: the "done" state always reflects reality; the "Waiting for..." indicator no longer appears on a reply that claims completion. - **Hygiene**: crashed or stale sessions become visible instead of silently accumulating over the day. - **Recoverability**: background-session results are not lost when a sync command moves to the background after a timeout. ## Environment - VS Code 1.140.0 (stable

title: node-api: objects from node_api_create_object_with_properties are in dictionary mode
excerpt: ### What is the problem this feature will solve? The new `node_api_create_object_with_properties` (#59953) always returns objects in dictionary mode. It calls `v8::Object::New(isolate, prototype, names, values, count)`, and V8 builds a dictionary there whatever the shape. So the objects are slow to read: about 8x slower than an object literal with `Object.prototype`, and about 75x with a `NULL` prototype, because then every object also gets its own map. `napi_create_object` plus `napi_define_properties` gives fast objects, but it costs about twice as much to build. So right now an addon can have cheap object creation or fast property access, not both. I measured it with a small addon: 10 properties, 100,000 objects, Node 26.10.0 on an M1 Max, median of 4 runs. The machine was busy, so the ratios matter more than the absolute numbers. Reads are compared with the object literal, builds with `node_api_create_object_with_properties` and `Object.prototype`. | | Fast properties | Read, ns per property | Build, ns per property | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | object literal | yes | 0.69 | 4.0 | | `napi_set_property` per property | yes, up to 19 properties | 0.82 (1.2x) | 117.5 (3.4x) | | `napi_define_properties` | yes | 0.79 (1.1x) | 70.3 (2.0x) | | `node_api_create_object_with_properties`, `Object.prototype` | **no** | **5.75 (8.3x)** | 34.9 | | `node_api_create_object_with_properties`, `NULL` | **no**, one map per object | **52.44 (75x)** | 45.7 (1.3x) | At 32 properties it looks the same, except that the `napi_set_property` objects are in dictionary mode too. Repro and raw output ```c #include #include enum { kWithProperties, kSetProperty, kDefineProperties }; // make(names, values, prototype, count[, how]): `count` objects, each from one // node_api_create_object_with_properties call (an undefined prototype passes NULL), or with // `how` 1 from napi_create_object and one napi_set_property call per property, or with `how` 2 // from napi_create_object and one napi_define_properties call (the prototype is ignored for both). static napi_value Make(napi_env env, napi_callback_info info) { size_t argc = 5; napi_value argv[5], result, proto; uint32_t width, count; int32_t how = kWithProperties; napi_valuetype type; napi_get_cb_info(env, info, &argc, argv, NULL, NULL); napi_get_array_length(env, argv[0], &width); napi_get_value_uint32(env, argv[3], &count); napi_typeof(env, argv[2], &type); proto = type == napi_undefined ? NULL : argv[2]; if (argc > 4) napi_get_value_int32(env, argv[4], &how); napi_value* names = malloc(sizeof(napi_value) * width * 2); napi_value* values = names + width; napi_property_descriptor* descriptors = calloc(width, sizeof(napi_property_descriptor)); for (uint32_t i = 0; i `k${i}`); const values = names.map((_, i) => i + 0.5); // Every case stores the same values; only the way the objects are made differs. const literals = new Function('n', 'v', ` const a = new Array(n); for (let i = 0; i `${k}: v[${j}]`).join(', ')} }; return a;`); co

title: Markdown links drop non-line fragments like #page=3 when opening files (PDF links always open on page 1)
excerpt: Does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: Not tested end to end. The drop happens in the built-in Markdown extension, so it does not depend on third-party extensions. Seeing the effect on a PDF needs a PDF viewer extension (see below). - VS Code Version: VS Code main as of 2026-09-30 - OS Version: macOS Following a markdown link to a non-text file with a non-line fragment, such as `[pdf](file.pdf#page=3)`, opens the file without the fragment, so a PDF viewer always starts on page 1. Only `L `-style fragments survive. Code path, from reading `extensions/markdown-language-features/src/util/openDocumentLink.ts` on main. The bundled `vscode-markdown-languageservice` 0.5.0 is the version pinned in `package.json`: 1. `MdLinkOpener.openDocumentLink` calls `resolveDocumentLink`, which sends `resolveLinkTarget` to the language server. 2. In the language service, `resolveLinkTarget` → `#resolveInternalLinkTarget` gets the fragment `page=3`. It is not a line/position fragment (`parseLocationInfoFromFragment` returns nothing) and the target is not a markdown document with a matching header, so it returns `{ kind: 'file', uri: target }`. `target` has no fragment. 3. `openResolvedDocumentLink` sees `resolved.kind === 'file'` and no `rangeSelection`, and `uri.fragment` is empty. So it calls `getLocationFragmentFromLinkText(linkText)`. That only accepts `^L?\d+(?:,\d+)?(?:-L?\d+(?:,\d+)?)?$`, so `page=3` returns `undefined` and the URI is left unchanged. 4. It then runs `vscode.commands.executeCommand('vscode.open', uri, { selection: undefined, viewColumn })` with a URI that has no `#page=3`. **Steps to Reproduce:** 1. Open a folder containing `doc.md` and any multi-page `file.pdf`. 2. In `doc.md` add `[pdf](file.pdf#page=3)`. 3. Install a PDF viewer extension that opens `.pdf` files in VS Code, for example "vscode-pdf" (`tomoki1207.pdf`). VS Code has no built-in PDF viewer. Whether a given viewer honors a URI fragment is up to that viewer. 4. Open the Markdown preview (`Markdown: Open Preview to the Side`) and click the link. Alternatively, Cmd+click the link in the editor. 5. To see the dropped fragment without any PDF viewer: open the repo in VS Code, run the "Run Extension" launch config, and set a breakpoint on the `vscode.open` call in `openResolvedDocumentLink` (`openDocumentLink.ts`). Repeat step 4 in the Extension Development Host and inspect `uri`. Expected per the code above: `uri.fragment` is `''`, and `uri.toString()` ends in `file.pdf` with no `#page=3`. **Expected:** the URI passed to `vscode.open` keeps the fragment (`file:///.../file.pdf#page=3`), so an editor or viewer that understands it can open at page 3. Line fragments such as `#L10` should keep working as before. **Actual:** the URI passed to `vscode.open` is `file:///.../file.pdf` and the fragment is lost, so the PDF opens at its default position (page 1). A fix is proposed in #332661.

title: Unnecessary lock in `bytearray.decode`
excerpt: In `bytearray.decode` it's implementation is protected with a critical section lock ``` skip_optional_pos: Py_BEGIN_CRITICAL_SECTION(self); return_value = bytearray_decode_impl((PyByteArrayObject *)self, encoding, errors); Py_END_CRITICAL_SECTION(); ``` However inside we call `PyUnicode_FromEncodedObject` -> `PyObject_GetBuffer` -> `bytearray_getbuffer` Where we fetch the lock again of itself. ``` static int bytearray_getbuffer(PyObject *self, Py_buffer *view, int flags) { int ret; Py_BEGIN_CRITICAL_SECTION(self); ret = bytearray_getbuffer_lock_held(self, view, flags); Py_END_CRITICAL_SECTION(); return ret; } ``` Calling getbuffer is required when the bytearray has been inherited however in the standard path we can look to skip the second getbuffer and it's associated lock. While working on a workshop about exception mode, the agent found that a function which catches exceptions had far fewer samples in `--mode exception` when called from a generator expression than when called from a plain loop, with nothing else changed. It reduced that to the script below and believes there is a disparity between what the documentation says exception mode records and what it actually records. title: Plugin marketplace: failed ref clone leaves an empty cache that blocks unpinned installs
excerpt: Found while testing #338175 / #337816. This is in the existing plugin repository/cache path, not established as a regression introduced by the installation-record PR. ## Environment - Code OSS 1.140.0 Dev, commit `9ae5e965fdd41026cd7bb60f232a339ea3c61761` - Windows x64, Git 2.55.0.windows.3, no sign-in - Disposable profile, explicit isolated `--agent-plugins-dir ` - `chat.customizations.marketplace.enabled: true`, `chat.plugins.enabled: true` - Plugin `microsoft-foundry` 1.0.0, source `./.github/plugins/microsoft-foundry` ## End-to-end reproduction 1. Use a fresh isolated plugin cache where ` /github.com/microsoft/skills` does not exist. 2. Configure `chat.plugins.marketplaces` with: ```json [ "github/awesome-copilot#marketplace", "microsoft/skills", "microsoft/skills#23d0dac5f83f268166a17f0bc7dc6c73dc348a33" ] ``` 3. Open Agent Customizations > Discover and search `microsoft-foundry`. 4. Install from the SHA-pinned `microsoft/skills#23d0dac...` source and accept trust. This currently fails because the SHA is passed to `git clone --branch` (a separate issue). 5. Inspect ` /github.com/microsoft/skills`: the failed `ref_ ` child is cleaned up, but its parent remains **empty**. 6. Install from the unpinned **microsoft/skills** source. Repeat with Retry Install. ## Actual The unpinned source keeps failing with: > Plugin source directory '.github/plugins/microsoft-foundry' not found in repository 'microsoft/skills'. No marketplace record is written and `installed.json` is not created. Retry does not recover the empty cache. Deleting **only the empty test cache directory** ` /github.com/microsoft/skills` and retrying recovered the installation. ## Expected A failed ref-specific clone must not poison an independent source's cache. An existing empty/non-repository folder should be validated/recovered, not treated as a successfully cloned repository. ## Diagnosis and confidence The ref-specific cache is nested inside the unpinned clone path: `.../skills/ref_ `. Code inspection suggests failed-clone cleanup removes only the child, while the unpinned repository lookup trusts folder existence instead of repository validity. The failure, empty parent, retry failure, and recovery were reproduced. A first occurrence also followed two cancelled clones, but which ref was cancelled and what initiated cancellation were not proven; the SHA-failure sequence above is the concrete repro.

title: API for language model providers to supply a model icon
excerpt: The chat model picker shows a provider icon next to each model's name (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, …). Extensions that contribute models through `LanguageModelChatProvider` have no way to choose that icon, so their models always get the generic sparkle. ### Current behavior - The icon comes from [`getProviderIconForIdentity()`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/widget/input/modelPicker/modelProviderIcons.ts#L28-L53), which looks for hard-coded strings in the model's vendor, family, id and name. - Any model from an extension other than Copilot that doesn't set the proposed `isBYOK` is [marked `isBYOK: true`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/api/browser/mainThreadLanguageModels.ts#L110-L115), and BYOK models [skip the string matching and get the sparkle](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/widget/input/modelPicker/modelProviderIcons.ts#L60-L62). Grok/xAI is the only exception. - The only override is the proposed [`statusIcon`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vscode-dts/vscode.proposed.chatProvider.d.ts#L79), which [takes precedence over the provider icon](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/widget/input/modelPicker/modelProviderIcons.ts#L71-L73). It's meant for model state (Copilot uses it for warnings), though, not identity. The [tests](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/test/browser/widget/input/modelPicker/modelProviderIcons.test.ts#L33-L69) show that VS Code deliberately avoids guessing a brand for BYOK models (e.g. a BYOK "Claude Sonnet 5" from vendor `anthropic` gets the generic icon). That makes sense when VS Code is the one doing the guessing. This request is for the provider to state its own icon explicitly, just as it already states `name` and `detail`. ### Motivation In the picker, the icon is how users tell models apart at a glance. Copilot-served models get recognizable icons, while every model from another extension looks identical. That's especially confusing for: - **Single-vendor providers** (an extension for one company's models), which want their own logo. - **Gateways and aggregators** (OpenRouter-style, enterprise proxies, self-hosted), which serve models from several upstream vendors through one extension and want per-model icons. - **Users with several providers installed**, who can't tell which extension a sparkle model comes from without opening its hover. ### Proposed shape One option is an optional per-model `iconPath` on `LanguageModelChatInformation`, using the existing [`IconPath`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vscode-dts/vsc

title: Finalize `LanguageModelChatInformation.statusIcon`
excerpt: `LanguageModelChatProvider` was finalized in #263415 (completing #250007). Two days later, #264061 added `statusIcon` to the `chatProvider` proposal, and it has stayed there ever since: ```ts // vscode.proposed.chatProvider.d.ts export interface LanguageModelChatInformation { // ... readonly statusIcon?: ThemeIcon; } ``` ([declaration](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vscode-dts/vscode.proposed.chatProvider.d.ts#L79); all links below are pinned to `1f64887`) Unlike its neighbours `isDefault` and `isUserSelectable`, it isn't marked "NOT BEING FINALIZED". Nothing seems to be tracking it, so I'd like to request finalization. ### Why it matters to extensions using only the stable API `statusIcon` isn't just decoration. In the language models management editor, the stable [`tooltip`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vscode-dts/vscode.d.ts#L20604) property is only shown in a model's hover when `statusIcon` is also set: [`getModelHoverContent()`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/chatManagement/chatModelsWidget.ts#L72) and [`ModelNameColumnRenderer.renderModelElement()`](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/1f6488722c942d1d7528a7d949769a69e4a557c3/src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/chatManagement/chatModelsWidget.ts#L635) both check `statusIcon && tooltip`. title: Docstring of array.array misses 'w' type info and mentions wide/narrow builds
excerpt: # Documentation The docstring of `array.array` at https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/cfcd52490d6531f3b0e8ddd4bb2b40fb6baee854/Modules/arraymodule.c#L2912 has a few mistakes: 1. in description of 'u' type it mentions the narrow/wide build split that is not a thing since 3.3 - https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.3.html#functionality 2. it doesn't mention that since 3.3 the 'u' type is deprecated and 'w' should be used. 3. it doesn't mention that 'u' type since 3.9 corresponds to `wchar_t` of C compiler used (so *usually* 2 byte UTF-16 on Windows, 4 byte UTF-32 elsewhere), instead of to narrow/wide Python build. 4. it doesn't mention the newer 'w' type that is Python's own `Py_UCS4` 4 byte UTF-32. The documentation at https://docs.python.org/3/library/array.html doesn't have these issues, only the docstring (that is shown in `help(array.array)` in the REPL) does. This is a mismatch between documentation and docstring. ### Linked PRs * gh-142323 * gh-158040 * gh-158575

title: Investigate Agent Host enforcement of content exclusions

title: Use source maps if extension ships one for error stack trace formatting
excerpt: In the [Julia extension]() we have crash reporting setup, so that we send a crash report whenever an exception occurs in our extension. We also bundle our extension with webpack. One problem is that the stack traces in the exceptions (if something goes wrong) are essentially useless, as they refer to locations in the bundled version of the extension, i.e. everything on line 1 :) We do actually ship a source map file in the extension, but the information in there doesn't show up in the exception objects. I think there are broadly speaking two ways to improve the situation: 1) run the extension host with the `--enable-source-maps` flag (but note that any custom `Error.prepareStackTrace` handler is then disabled, or 2) modify the already existing `Error.prepareStackTrace` handler in the extension host https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/32b031eeefc4fd27a21659d35070967bfe965bcc/src/vs/workbench/api/common/extensionHostMain.ts#L92 to apply source map information if it is there. I am experimenting with that at the moment by using the https://www.npmjs.com/package/source-map-support package in our extension. That actually _does_ lead to error objects that have stack traces that use the source map information, so that is great. The drawback, though, is that by using this package I think we are overriding the default VS Code `Error.prepareStackTrace` handler that gets set [here](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/blob/32b031eeefc4fd27a21659d35070967bfe965bcc/src/vs/workbench/api/common/extensionHostMain.ts#L92), and potentially even for not just our extension? That seems really bad, but at the moment I don't really have a better idea on how to handle that... I think the ideal situation is that the default `Error.prepareStackTrace` that the VS Code extension hosts installs essentially provides the same functionality that the `source-map-support` package provides.

title: API proposal: Expose AuthenticationSession access token lifetime
excerpt: ## Problem `AuthenticationSession` exposes an access token but not its lifetime. Consumers that integrate with SDKs supporting renewable credentials cannot tell whether a token is static or when it should be refreshed. #152517 previously proposed exposing an absolute `expiresAt` timestamp. An absolute timestamp is unsafe across VS Code's client/remote extension-host boundary because the two machines may have clock skew. ## Proposed API ```ts export interface AuthenticationSession { /** * The access token's remaining lifetime, in milliseconds, when the authentication provider returns the session. * * This corresponds to `expires_in` in an OAuth 2.0 token response, converted from seconds to * milliseconds. Providers returning cached sessions must recompute this value. This is undefined * when the authentication provider does not know the access token's expiry. When defined, this * must be a positive integer. */ readonly expiresAfter?: number; } ``` ## Semantics - The value is a positive integer representing whole milliseconds remaining when the session is returned. - Cached sessions recompute the value on every return. - `undefined` means the provider does not know the token's expiry. - The relative lifetime avoids comparing clocks across extension-host boundaries. ## Implementation The proposal lives in `vscode.proposed.authSessionExpiration.d.ts`. #334418 added it as `expiresIn` in seconds, and #335610 renamed it to `expiresAfter` in milliseconds. The GitHub Authentication extension reports it for Entra-brokered sessions, and the Microsoft Authentication extension reports MSAL token expiry. Related to #152517.

title: Support expiring GitHub tokens with the offline_access scope
excerpt: GitHub sessions only expire today when they're brokered through Microsoft Entra (#335183). Those sessions report `expiresAfter` and renew themselves before they run out. Ordinary GitHub OAuth sessions are stored in the keychain with no known expiry, and nothing ever renews them. The GitHub Authentication extension should support expiring GitHub tokens for those sessions too, by requesting the `offline_access` scope. With `offline_access`, sign-in returns an access token that expires plus a refresh token. The extension would: - store the refresh token next to the session - report the access token's remaining lifetime through `expiresAfter` - renew the access token before it expires, the same way Entra-brokered sessions renew today The renewal path in `extensions/github-authentication/src/github.ts` (`stillGood`) only handles transient Entra-brokered sessions. It will need to give persisted sessions their own expiry and branch on how a given session renews. Related: #335183, #335184

title: GitHub Authentication: Support expiring GitHub tokens brokered through Microsoft Entra
excerpt: ## Problem The GitHub Authentication extension can broker GitHub access tokens through a signed-in Microsoft Entra account. These exchanged GitHub tokens have a finite lifetime, but the extension previously treated them like ordinary persisted GitHub OAuth tokens with no known expiry or renewal path. Once an exchanged token expired, consumers could lose authentication and fall back to an interactive sign-in prompt even though the Microsoft account was still signed in and could silently mint a replacement. ## Desired behavior - Keep the exchanged token's absolute expiry internally. - Return its current relative lifetime through `AuthenticationSession.expiresIn`. - Recompute the remaining lifetime whenever a cached session is returned. - Silently renew Microsoft-brokered GitHub sessions before expiry, including the one-hour threshold required by the Copilot SDK. - Coalesce concurrent renewal attempts. - Retain a still-valid token when proactive renewal fails transiently, and only remove the session after the token actually expires. - Leave ordinary persisted GitHub OAuth sessions unchanged when their expiry is unknown. ## Implementation Implemented by #334418, including mocked coverage for initial exchange, restore, cached lifetime recomputation, renewal, and transient renewal failures.

title: Agent Host: Support expiring GitHub tokens with the Copilot SDK
excerpt: ## Problem Agent Host currently supplies a static GitHub token when creating Copilot SDK sessions. Some GitHub tokens have a known finite lifetime, and the Copilot SDK supports a `gitHubTokenProvider` callback for refreshing those credentials. Without carrying token lifetime to Agent Host and selecting the provider callback, a long-running Copilot session can continue using an expired token or surface an interactive authentication prompt instead of requesting a fresh credential. ## Desired behavior - Carry optional OAuth-style `expiresIn` through Agent Host authentication and reconnect/replay. - Deduct elapsed time when credentials are replayed and do not replay expired credentials. - Use a static `gitHubToken` when expiry is unknown. - Use `gitHubTokenProvider` when expiry is known, never both options at once. - Coalesce concurrent SDK refresh callbacks and map refresh requests to the existing Agent Host authentication-required flow. - Bound refresh waits so the SDK cannot wait indefinitely when no client supplies a replacement. - Restart the Copilot client when switching between static and provider-backed credential modes. ## Implementation Implemented by #334418, with unit coverage for credential selection, refresh coalescing, timeout behavior, replay, and mode transitions. The refresh path was also validated end to end with a real Microsoft-brokered GitHub token renewal.

title: vm: timeout during an afterEvaluate microtask checkpoint corrupts the async hook stack
excerpt: ### Version v27.0.0-nightly20261001cede7e6740 (also v26.10.0, v24.21.0, v24.18.0) ### Platform ```text Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 ``` ### Subsystem vm, async_hooks ### What steps will reproduce the bug? ```js const async_hooks = require('node:async_hooks'); const vm = require('node:vm'); async_hooks.createHook({ init() {} }).enable(); const context = vm.createContext({}, { microtaskMode: 'afterEvaluate' }); try { vm.runInContext('Promise.resolve().then(() => { while (true); })', context, { timeout: 5 }); } catch (error) { console.log('caught:', error.code); } setImmediate(() => console.log('survived')); ``` Run it with `node repro.js`. The explicit hook only arms Node's async-stack check. `node --test` arms the same check, so the snippet also fails without the hook when its body runs inside `test()`. ### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition? Every run: 3 of 3 on each listed version. It requires a context created with `microtaskMode: 'afterEvaluate'`, a `timeout` (or `breakOnSigint`) that fires while a microtask runs during the post-evaluation checkpoint, and an enabled async hook. Without an enabled hook the process survives. ### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior? ```text caught: ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT survived ``` The timeout is documented to throw `ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT` to the caller, and the caller does catch it. Afterwards the process should continue normally. ### What do you see instead? The timeout is caught, then the process exits with status 1 at the next callback scope: ```text caught: ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT Error: async hook stack has become corrupted (actual: 3, expected: 1) ----- Native stack trace ----- 1: node::AsyncHooks::FailWithCorruptedAsyncStack(double) 2: node::AsyncHooks::pop_async_context(double) 3: node::InternalCallbackScope::Close() 4: node::InternalCallbackScope::~InternalCallbackScope() 5: node::StartExecution(...) ``` Other placements fail with `execution_async_id() == 0` or the same corruption message. ### Additional information In `ContextifyScript::EvalMachine`, `PerformCheckpoint` for an `afterEvaluate` context runs inside the watchdog scope. When the watchdog terminates a promise job, the job's async-hook `before` callback has already pushed its async context, but its `after` callback never pops it. `CancelTerminateExecution` then returns with the async-id stack deeper than it was at entry to `EvalMachine`. This is the mechanism analysed in #38503. That issue was closed by 4f844f4 (`repl: use inspector over vm`), which removed the REPL trigger. The `vm` defect itself is still present on `main`, as the nightly above shows. A possible fix: record the stack length on entry and, after cancelling this invocation's own termination, pop contexts back to that length. title: Add an external flag to interpreter frames
excerpt: ### Feature or enhancement I would like to add an `external` flag to the _PyInterpreterFrame struct. This would be a single bit, bit-packed into the same uint8_t that the currently unused `visited` flag is already occupying. When anything besides the VM pushes a frame onto the frame stack (for example, anyone using the long-blessed PEP 523 evaluators or writing JITs), oftentimes there is metadata associated with those frames that needs correlation. In order to make that correlation, we need to know if a frame is associated with an external source. There are a couple of ways to solve this, but every solution that doesn't involve storing something on the frame itself involves maintaining a separate data structure and mutating it on every activation. This becomes especially difficult when dealing with arbitrary frames, for example from the perspective of either GC or a profiler/debugger. The ideal solution involves having a bit on the interpreter frame that indicates it's safe to read some other data structure containing the metadata. For example, we could stack allocate the metadata immediately before the interpreter frame, and this bit proves it's safe to read. This should have zero impact on memory, since it's using an existing bit. It should also have zero impact on performance until the point that the `visited` flag is actually used, at which point it should be negligible since it will be one additional mask. ### Has this already been discussed elsewhere? This is a minor feature, which does not need previous discussion elsewhere ### Links to previous discussion of this feature: _No response_ cc @DinoV @markshannon ### Linked PRs * gh-158573

title: ProcessPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True) deadlocks when worker exit messages fill the result pipe
excerpt: ### Bug report `ProcessPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True)` can hang forever when the pool has many workers. When shutting down, `_ExecutorManagerThread._join_executor_internals()` sends one `None` sentinel per worker and then calls `p.join()` on every worker. Each worker handles its sentinel by calling `result_queue.put(os.getpid())` in `_process_worker` before it exits. By then the manager thread has stopped reading `result_queue`, so nothing drains it while it waits in `join()`. Once the result pipe is full, the next exiting worker blocks in `write()` while holding the queue's write lock. All remaining workers then block on that lock, and `join()` never returns. Each exit message is about 21 bytes, so a default 64 KiB pipe only fills with roughly 3000 workers. On Linux, however an unprivileged user who is over `fs.pipe-user-pages-soft` gets new pipes at the minimum size only 1/2 Pages. This is low enough to be high on high core count machines that run many processes. I found this when running LLVM's `lit` test runner on a 512-thread machine. All tests finished, then `shutdown()` hung with 464 workers. At that point 389 workers had exited, one was blocked in `pipe_write`, and the rest were waiting on the queue's write lock. Reproducer. `F_SETPIPE_SZ` is only used to simulate the small-pipe fallback deterministically: ```python import concurrent.futures import fcntl import multiprocessing F_SETPIPE_SZ = 1031 def init(barrier): global _barrier _barrier = barrier def work(_): _barrier.wait() # every worker must be running a task at the same time if __name__ == "__main__": n = 400 ex = concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor( max_workers=n, initializer=init, initargs=(multiprocessing.Barrier(n),)) fcntl.fcntl(ex._result_queue._writer.fileno(), F_SETPIPE_SZ, 4096) list(ex.map(work, range(n))) # all n workers are now alive ex.shutdown(wait=True) # hangs print("done") ``` With `n = 100` this finishes in about 0.03s. With `n = 400` it hangs on 3.10.11, 3.12.3, 3.13.15, 3.14.7 and main. Without the `F_SETPIPE_SZ` call, it also hangs when run by a user who is over `pipe-user-pages-soft`. Stack of the manager thread while hung (main): ``` File ".../multiprocessing/process.py", line 156 in join File ".../concurrent/futures/process.py", line 684 in _join_executor_internals File ".../concurrent/futures/process.py", line 667 in join_executor_internals ``` Proposed fix: keep draining the result queue while joining the workers in `_join_executor_internals()`. When that point is reached there is also no work items left as such we can drain them safely. I have a patch that fixes it with a regression test and will open a PR shortly. *The analysis and reproducer were prepared with help from an AI assistant (Claude). I reviewed and verified them.* ### CPython versions tested on: 3.10, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, CPython main branch ### Operating systems tested on: Linux ### Linked PRs * gh-158571

title: unavoidable spurious "exception in shielded future" logged if exception raised after shield cancelled
excerpt: # Bug report ### Bug description: test case: ```python import asyncio async def fail(t): await asyncio.sleep(1) raise ValueError("should be caught, not logged") async def main(): fut = asyncio.create_task(fail(1)) try: await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(fut), timeout=0.5) except asyncio.TimeoutError: print("timeout, as expected") try: await fut except Exception as e: print("error caught and handled:", e) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` #134331 appears to have introduced a regression where `_log_on_exception` is added [_unconditionally and permanently_](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/ee1da7ec8e939a998d5ecf2c749d45eb8f7714e4/Lib/asyncio/tasks.py#L997) on a future that has been shielded at some point, when the shield future is cancelled, rather than removing the handler when the shield future is done. In the above code, a long-running future is created. `shield` It is awaited with a timeout using `wait_for(shield(fut))`. Since the future is not done, this completes and should leave us in a state just like we had an `asyncio.sleep(0.5)`. However, instead when the future resolves, the error is logged, even though the exception is caught and handled: ``` > python3 test.py timeout, as expected ValueError exception in shielded future future: exception=ValueError('should be caught, not logged')> Traceback (most recent call last): File "/tmp/test.py", line 5, in fail raise ValueError("should be caught, not logged") ValueError: should be caught, not logged error caught and handled: should be caught, not logged ``` as far as I can tell, the behavior is more correct if `_log_on_exception` is removed entirely, but I don't fully track #134331, so it may be solving a problem I don't see. Maybe I'm missing something? Is there some assumption that the inner future should always be finished before the outer one unless something is wrong? That's what the logging behavior suggests to me. This is a regression in 3.14. 3.13 and prior appear to have correct logging behavior for failure after shielding. ### CPython versions tested on: 3.14 ### Operating systems tested on: macOS ### Linked PRs * gh-156521

title: Remove unnecessary loads "critical_section" from `_PyCriticalSection_SuspendAll`
excerpt: Compilers were unable to prove that the value at this address will not change, and they do not keep the previously loaded value live across the call; as a result, they reload it both in the `or` rmw operation and when checking `two mutex`. To avoid reloading the value multiple times, we store it once in a register; this prevents the compilers from performing unnecessary load operations, allowing them to simply read the value and perform the OR operation on it. Of course, this puts additional pressure on the registers (in this case, callee-saved), but since they are callee-saved anyway, calls to other functions would save our registers regardless, we simply store our cached `critical_section` value in them; additionally, the extra `push` operations shouldn’t be a problem, since they likely fit into the same cache line, so when flushing values, this can be a single cache line flush. Also, here we only pay the cost of the extra registers once, at the beginning of the function. The previous version, on the other hand, re-reads the values each time, so the number of `load` operations is proportional to the number of `critical_section`s we iterate through. ``` Configured with: ../configure CC=clang CXX=clang++ \ --disable-gil --enable-optimizations Built with: make ``` before: ```c void _PyCriticalSection_SuspendAll(PyThreadState *tstate) { #ifdef Py_GIL_DISABLED uintptr_t *tagptr = &tstate->critical_section; title: _pyrepl: Reader.suspend() discards buffer, pos, and kill_ring
excerpt: ### Bug description: `Reader.suspend()` captures all 29 fields of the reader, but only restores 6 of them (`msg`, `ps1`–`ps4`, `paste_mode`). The `self.prepare()` call in the `finally` block clears `self.buffer`, resets `self.pos`, and clears `self.kill_ring`, and those are not restored. ### Reproducer: ```python from _pyrepl.reader import Reader class FakeConsole: height = 24 width = 80 input_hook = None def prepare(self): pass def restore(self): pass def refresh(self, screen): pass def move_cursor(self, x, y): pass def finish(self): pass def wait(self, timeout): return False def get_event(self, block=False): return None def push_char(self, c): pass def getheightwidth(self): return (self.height, self.width) r = Reader(FakeConsole()) r.buffer[:] = list("hello world") r.pos = 5 r.kill_ring.append(list("saved")) before = (list(r.buffer), r.pos, [list(k) for k in r.kill_ring]) with r.suspend(): pass after = (list(r.buffer), r.pos, [list(k) for k in r.kill_ring]) print(f"before: {before}") print(f"after: {after}") Expected: suspend() should be transparent: after the context manager exits, the reader should be in the same state as before, apart from the fields that the nested reader is allowed to change. Actual: The buffer is empty, pos is 0, and kill_ring is cleared. Reachability: Reader.suspend() is called by help (F1) in Lib/_pyrepl/commands.py: python class help(Command): def do(self) -> None: import _sitebuiltins with self.reader.suspend(): self.reader.msg = _sitebuiltins._Helper()() self.reader.invalidate_prompt() and wrapped by HistoricalReader.suspend() in Lib/_pyrepl/historical_reader.py: python @contextmanager def suspend(self) -> SimpleContextManager: with super().suspend(), self.suspend_history(): yield ``` A user who types something and then presses F1 loses their input. title: 3.14: objects de-immortalized by old stable-ABI extensions break truthiness checks in specialized bytecode
excerpt: # Bug report ### Bug description: Extensions compiled against 3.11 or older headers implement `Py_DECREF` as an inline `--ob_refcnt`. That includes abi3 wheels built on 3.11, which are common. Since 3.12 the interpreter hands out references to immortal objects without incrementing their refcount, so each such reference the extension releases is a net decrement. 3.14 starts immortal objects at `3 << 30` and treats `(int32_t)ob_refcnt < 0` as immortal, which leaves a margin of 2**30 (see gh-125174). That margin runs out in real long-running processes. Home Assistant on 3.14.6 crashes after hours to days because PyAV's `cp311-abi3` wheels drain `True` by a few counts per `av.open()` and per FFmpeg log line (https://github.com/PyAV-Org/PyAV/issues/2420, https://github.com/home-assistant/core/issues/178218). A core dump from an affected instance had `_Py_TrueStruct.ob_refcnt == 0x7ffb2327`, which is 2**30 + 318,681 below `0xC0000000`. On 3.12 and 3.13, losing immortality is fairly benign: the object is then refcounted like any other, and results stay correct. On 3.14 it is a silent correctness failure. The reason is in the default build's stackrefs: - `PyStackRef_IsTrue`/`IsFalse`/`IsNone` compare the tagged bits exactly. - `_PyStackRef_FromPyObjectNew` and `PyStackRef_MakeHeapSafe` decide whether to tag with `_Py_IsImmortal()`, which reads the refcount. - `PyStackRef_FromPyObjectSteal` decides with `ob_flags`. Once `True`'s refcount is below 2**31, a `True` loaded by a specialized attribute load (`LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE` and others) or passed through `RETURN_VALUE` is untagged, and `POP_JUMP_IF_TRUE` treats it as false. `True` from constants, comparisons and C calls still tests true, so the failures look random. In Home Assistant, `Thread.name` asserted `Thread.__init__() not called`, `Condition.notify` raised `cannot notify on un-acquired lock`, `traceback` printed `None` as the exception type, and so on, across threads, until the process exited. Reproducer. `ctypes` stands in for the extension's unbalanced decrefs: ```python import ctypes, sys print(sys.version) class C: def __init__(self): self.flag = True def check_attr(o): if not o.flag: # LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE, POP_JUMP_IF_TRUE return "WRONG: o.flag is True but tested false" return "ok" def get_true(): return True def check_return(): if not get_true(): # CALL_PY_EXACT_ARGS, RETURN_VALUE, POP_JUMP_IF_TRUE return "WRONG: get_true() returned True but tested false" return "ok" o = C() for _ in range(1000): # warm up so both functions get specialized check_attr(o), check_return() refcnt = ctypes.c_uint32.from_address(id(True)) # low 32 bits of ob_refcnt (64-bit little-endian) print("before: ob_refcnt = %#x" % refcnt.value, check_attr(o), check_return()) refcnt.value = 2**31 - 10**6 # 3.14: 2**30 + 10**6 raw decrements from 0xc0000000 print("after: ob_refcnt = %#x" % refcnt.value, check_attr(o), check_return()) print("o.flag is True:", o.flag is True, "| bool(o.flag):", bool(o.flag)) ``` Output

title: `tomllib` reports an error position beyond EOF for some files ending in backslash
excerpt: ## Bug description This is a fairly minor bug in `tomllib`: when a document ends with an unfinished backslash escape inside a double-quoted string or key, the exception reports that the error is *past* the end of the document. ```python import tomllib document = '"\\' # A quote followed by a backslash. try: tomllib.loads(document) except tomllib.TOMLDecodeError as exc: print(len(exc.doc), exc.pos, exc.lineno, exc.colno) # 2 3 1 4 # Doc length = 2 # Error position = 3 (1 past the EOF) # Line number = 1 (correct) # Column number = 4 (1 past EOF) ``` The document has two characters, but `pos` is 3. I would expect the position to point either to the backslash or to EOF, which would be index 2 and column 3. As a practical matter the formatted message already says "at end of document", so this only affects callers using the location attributes. The same thing happens for a trailing backslash in a basic string value or a multiline basic string. An unterminated string without the backslash, such as `'"abc'`, reports `pos == len(doc)` as expected. The cause is [`parse_basic_str_escape`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/eb30e3d9d4b523e3f8de2cd1485c9ae9a996ab03/Lib/tomllib/_parser.py#L566-L594) advancing the position by two before checking the escape, even when only the backslash remains. That position is then used to construct `TOMLDecodeError`. I found this while adding Hypothesis tests in [gh-158565](https://github.com/python/cpython/pull/158565). The PR includes a focused expected-failure property and the minimized example above. This is related to but distinct from [Tomli #307](https://github.com/hukkin/tomli/pull/307), which concerns the location reported for invalid Unicode escape digits. ## CPython versions tested on - Python 3.14.7. - Main at `eb30e3d9d4b523e3f8de2cd1485c9ae9a996ab03`, using a local Python 3.16.0a0 build to run that checkout's `tomllib`. ## Operating systems tested on Linux.

title: module.enableCompileCache() never returns on Windows for some cache-directory lengths (spins at 100% CPU)
excerpt: ### Version v24.18.0 ### Platform Microsoft Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, x64. `LongPathsEnabled` = 1. ### Subsystem module (compile cache) ### What steps will reproduce the bug? Run this PowerShell script. It calls `module.enableCompileCache()` on directories of different lengths under `%TEMP%`, and kills any call that has not returned after 6 seconds. ```powershell $base = Join-Path $env:TEMP 'cc-repro' New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $base | Out-Null foreach ($len in 200, 220, 230, 240, 245, 250, 260, 300) { $p = $base; $i = 0 while ($p.Length -lt $len) { $p = Join-Path $p ("d" + ($i++)) } $p = $p.Substring(0, $len).TrimEnd('\') $psi = [System.Diagnostics.ProcessStartInfo]::new('node.exe') $psi.Arguments = "-e `"const r=require('module').enableCompileCache(process.argv[1]);console.log(r.status+' '+(r.message||''))`" `"$p`"" $psi.UseShellExecute = $false; $psi.RedirectStandardOutput = $true $proc = [System.Diagnostics.Process]::Start($psi) if (-not $proc.WaitForExit(6000)) { $proc.Kill(); "{0} chars: HANG" -f $p.Length } else { "{0} chars: {1}" -f $p.Length, $proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEnd().Trim() } } ``` ### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition? It happens every time for directory lengths 240 and 245, with `%TEMP%` under `C:\Users\ \AppData\Local\Temp`. The exact lengths that hang depend on the path's structure. In our case a real 283-character cache path also hung, while the synthetic 282-character path above fails cleanly. ### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior? `enableCompileCache()` should return. It should either enable the cache or report failure, as it does for every other length: ``` 200 chars: 1 220 chars: 1 230 chars: 0 Cannot create cache directory: no such file or directory 234 chars: 0 Cannot create cache directory: no such file or directory 240 chars: HANG 245 chars: HANG 250 chars: 0 Cannot create cache directory: no such file or directory 260 chars: 0 Cannot create cache directory: no such file or directory 300 chars: 0 Cannot create cache directory: no such file or directory ``` ### What do you see instead? The call never returns. The main thread spins inside native code: - One core runs at 100%. - Process I/O counters show about 150,000 file-system metadata operations a second (`OtherOperationCount`), with no writes. - Timers never fire, and the inspector cannot pause the thread, so neither `--cpu-prof` nor `Debugger.pause` produces a stack. - A `--prof` tick profile attributes about 99% of ticks to `ntdll.dll` under the calling script. The same hang occurs when the cache is enabled through the `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` environment variable. In a worker thread, that variable also freezes a main thread that is waiting on the worker. ### Additional information We hit this in production: an application enabled the compile cache in its launcher, its entry module and its worker threads, using a cache path built from a long build ID. title: sys.setrecursionlimit docs are incorrect in 3.12 and 3.13
excerpt: Since 3.12, `sys.setrecursionlimit` does not control the recursion limit of the C stack (it's hardcoded in `Py_C_RECURSION_LIMIT`, due to #91079), while the [3.13 docs](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/sys.html#sys.setrecursionlimit) say ``` Set the maximum depth of the Python interpreter stack to limit. This limit prevents infinite recursion from causing an overflow of the C stack and crashing Python. ``` The fallout can be seen in #112215 (basically, any code that uses `lru_cache` in combination with `sys.setrecursionlimit` is potentially, or actually, broken in 3.12, while still working in 3.11) or in #107263 (which was papered over with an increase of `Py_C_RECURSION_LIMIT`, not really fixed). This is an obvious change of behaviour, as code working in 3.11 can easily be broken in 3.12, as found in #112215 ```python import sys sys.setrecursionlimit(1001) from functools import cache @cache def fib(n): if n ", line 15, in File " ", line 13, in fib File " ", line 13, in fib File " ", line 13, in fib [Previous line repeated 496 more times] RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ``` Such changes should carry a warning in the documentation. Potentially, any recursive Python code combining C recursion (in a module, e.g. `lru_cache`, via `@lru_cache` decorator) with increased (beyond the hardcoded `Py_C_RECURSION_LIMIT`) `sys.setrecursionlimit` is bound to be broken in 3.12. I believe the whole hardcoding of `Py_C_RECURSION_LIMIT` has to be fixed (perhaps with a separate API provided to change it), as it's a regression and an incompatible change of code behaviour, but meanwhile the docs have to reflect the reality.

title: Rewrite `turtle`'s undo handling to fix various issues
excerpt: There are currently three bugs in `turtle`'s undo handling. 1. `stamp()` fails when the undo buffer is disabled ```python import turtle t = turtle.Turtle() t.setundobuffer(None) t.stamp() # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'push' ``` `clearstamp()`, `clear()` and `reset()` fail the same way if a stamp exists when the buffer is disabled. 2. `teleport()` is not recorded in the undo buffer ```python import turtle t = turtle.Turtle() t.forward(50) t.teleport(0, 100) t.undo() print(t.pos()) # (0.00,100.00), expected (50.00,0.00) t.undo() t.undo() # also prints "undogoto: HALLO-DA-STIMMT-WAS-NICHT!" ...? ``` Only the pen changes made by `teleport()` are undone, never the move itself, so undoing earlier moves starts from the wrong position. 3. An exception in `write()`, `circle()` or `dot()` corrupts later undo steps ```python import turtle t = turtle.Turtle() try: t.write("hi", align="middle") # KeyError except KeyError: pass t.forward(10) t.forward(10) t.undo() print(t.pos()) # (0.00,0.00), expected (10.00,0.00) ``` These methods set `undobuffer.cumulate = True` and only reset it on success, so after an error every later action is merged into a single undo step. I propose adding a private context manager that `circle()`, `dot()`, `write()` and `teleport()` can use to group their actions into one undo step, so an exception can no longer leave the undo buffer merging every later action, and for `teleport()` to records its move so a single `undo()` reverts it. Also we need to guard `stamp()`, `clearstamp()`, `clear()` and `reset()` against a disabled undo buffer. ### Linked PRs * gh-158564

title: re.search() misses matches when a pattern starts with a scoped (?a:...) or (?u:...) group
excerpt: ### Bug description: `search()` (and so `findall()`, `finditer()`, `sub()`, `split()`) can miss a match that `match()` finds at the same position. It happens when the pattern starts with a scoped type-flag group, `(?a:...)` or `(?u:...)`, whose flag differs from the pattern's own: ```pycon >>> import re >>> p = re.compile(r'(?u:\w)', re.ASCII) >>> p.match('é') >>> print(p.search('é')) None >>> re.findall(r'(?u:\w)', 'café', re.ASCII) ['c', 'a', 'f'] >>> re.match(r'(?a:\W)', 'ß') >>> print(re.search(r'(?a:\W)', 'ß')) None >>> re.findall(r'(?a:\W)', 'Straße!') ['!'] >>> re.findall(r'(?a:\W)|x', 'Straße!') # an alternative disables the prefilter, and the result changes ['ß', '!'] ``` **Cause.** `_compile_info()` builds the "charset" prefilter that `SRE(search)` uses to skip start positions. `_get_charset_prefix()` looks through leading groups and combines their flags (`Lib/re/_optimizer.py:331` on main at a57d16507cccb69d3d76ae05b52f01627d0bc479). It returns only the charset, though, and `_compile_info()` compiles that charset with the pattern's own flags (`:428`). A category escape inside the group (`\w`, `\W`, `\d`, `\D`, `\s`, `\S`) therefore gets the pattern's character type in the prefilter and the group's type in the pattern body. `re.DEBUG` shows the mismatch (3.14.5): ``` >>> re.compile(r'(?u:\w)', re.ASCII | re.DEBUG) SUBPATTERN None 32 0 IN CATEGORY CATEGORY_WORD 0. INFO 7 0b100 1 1 (to 8) in 5. CATEGORY WORD = pos` where `match(s, i)` succeeds. Unpatched: 8 cases broke that rule, all with a scoped type-flag group. Patched: 0. - On main (333071231d), with the fix applied to `Lib/re/_optimizer.py`: the regression test fails before and passes after; `test_re` 171 ran, 0 failures, 4 skipped; and the same search-vs-match rule over 320,000 generated cases (2 seeds; lookaround / `\b` / anchor / `\s+` leads, nested `a`/`u`/`i` groups, str patterns) gives 1,338 violations with main's own `_optimizer.py` and 0 with the fix. ### CPython versions tested on: 3.12, 3.13, 3.14, CPython main branch ### Operating systems tested on: Linux --- AI assistance was used to investigate this and to draft this report. ### Linked PRs * gh-158375

title: `re` docs never say that the ASCII flag affects `\p{...}` properties
excerpt: ### Documentation https://docs.python.org/dev/library/re.html#re.A The `re.ASCII` entry lists `\w`, `\W`, `\b`, `\B`, `\d`, `\D`, `\s` and `\S` as the constructs it restricts, and the `\p{property=value}` section never mentions the flags. Six accepted property spellings are restricted by the flag as well, because `Nd`, `digit`, `word`, `space`, `White_Space` and `WSpace` are matched with the same engine categories as `\d`, `\s` and `\w`. The other 52 accepted spellings are unaffected. ``` $ cat repro.py import re s = '0\u0663 \xa0x' for p in 'Nd', 'digit', 'word', 'space', 'White_Space', 'WSpace': pat = r'\p{%s}' % p print('%-12s %-18r %r' % (p, re.findall(pat, s), re.findall(pat, s, re.ASCII))) $ ./python repro.py Nd ['0', '٣'] ['0'] digit ['0', '٣'] ['0'] word ['0', '٣', 'x'] ['0', 'x'] space [' ', '\xa0'] [' '] White_Space [' ', '\xa0'] [' '] WSpace [' ', '\xa0'] [' '] ``` Expected: the `\p{property=value}` section says which properties the ASCII flag restricts, alongside the existing note that `space` follows `str.isspace` and `xdigit` matches only the ASCII hexadecimal digits. `\p{White_Space}` and `\p{WSpace}` are also absent from the documented list of supported properties, although both are accepted. ### Linked PRs * gh-157699

title: netrc.__repr__() doesnt quote values, so its output often cant be parsed back
excerpt: # Bug report ### Bug description: `netrc.__repr__()` says it dumps the data "in the format of a .netrc file", but it writes every value as is with no quoting. So the output only parses back if every value is a single non empty word. The simplest case is an entry with no login, which is pretty normal for token based logins: ```python import netrc, tempfile from pathlib import Path with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d: p = Path(d) / "netrc" p.write_text("machine example.com password hunter2\n") n = netrc.netrc(p) print(n.hosts) # {'example.com': ('', '', 'hunter2')} print(repr(n).splitlines()) # ['machine example.com', '\tlogin ', '\tpassword hunter2'] p.write_text(repr(n)) netrc.netrc(p) # NetrcParseError: bad follower token 'hunter2' ``` The empty login gets written as `login ` followed by nothing, so the parser takes `password` as the login and then chokes on `hunter2`. Same thing with other values, i tried a few as the password: ``` "pass word" -> NetrcParseError: bad follower token 'word' "pass\tword" -> NetrcParseError "pass\nword" -> NetrcParseError " pass" -> reads back as 'pass' "pass\word" -> reads back as 'password' ``` The last two are the worst ones since nothing fails, you just get a different password back. The reader in the same file already supports quoted values and backslash escapes (`_netrclex.get_token`), the writer just never uses them. Looks like this goes back to GH-2491 (bpo-30806, #74989). Before that `__repr__` used `repr()` for the values and that fix replaced it with plain f-strings, with the commit message saying "netrc file format doesn't support quotes and escapes". But `_netrclex` does support both, so the Python quotes got removed and nothing replaced them. That fix also added a round trip check to the tests: ```python nrc2 = self.make_nrc(nrc.__repr__()) self.assertEqual(nrc.hosts, nrc2.hosts) ``` but it was dropped in GH-26330 (15409c720b) when `test_default` was rewritten, and nothing in `test_netrc.py` calls `__repr__` now. A fix would be to quote a value when its empty or has whitespace, `"` or `\` in it, and escape `\` and `"` inside the quotes the way `_netrclex` reads them. One thing to keep in mind is #99080 (backslashes outside quotes get dropped by the parser), if that changes how backslashes are read the escaping here would have to match. I have a patch with a round trip test for all the cases above, happy to open a PR. ### CPython versions tested on: CPython main branch, 3.13 ### Operating systems tested on: Windows ### Linked PRs * gh-158561

title: inspect.getsourcelines raises TokenError for lambda following a multiline string closing delimiter
excerpt: ### Bug description `inspect.getsourcelines()` raises `tokenize.TokenError` for a lambda defined on the same line as the closing delimiter of a multiline string, even when the complete, valid source file is available. Save the following as `repro.py` and run it from a file: ```python import inspect pair = ( """text """, lambda: None ) print(inspect.getsourcelines(pair[1])) ``` On CPython 3.14.7 and 3.15.0rc2, the final exception is: ```text tokenize.TokenError: ('EOF in multi-line string', (1, 1)) ``` Expected behavior: return the source lines containing the lambda without a tokenization error. The file is valid Python, and the lambda itself works normally. The lambda's `co_firstlineno` correctly points to the line containing `lambda`, which also contains the multiline string's closing delimiter. `getsourcelines()` passes the source slice starting on this line to `getblock()`. Tokenizing that slice loses the opening delimiter, so the closing delimiter is interpreted as the beginning of a new multiline string. Moving the lambda onto a separate line avoids the failure. In a larger reproduction containing another triple-quoted string later in the file, inspection can instead return an oversized, incorrect source block. An equivalent example was also reproduced on CPython 3.8.20, 3.9.25, 3.10.19, 3.11.14, 3.12.12, and 3.13.13. All raised `TokenError`, with minor differences in the reported error location. Related reports include #88640 (truncated multiline lambda bodies) and #143299 (adjacent code on shared source lines). title: date.fromisoformat() silently ignores the last two characters of a 10-character basic-format string
excerpt: # Bug report ### Bug description: `date.fromisoformat()` accepts a 10-character string in basic format and silently drops its last two characters: ```pycon >>> from datetime import date, datetime >>> date.fromisoformat('2020010112') # e.g. a YYYYMMDDHH stamp datetime.date(2020, 1, 1) >>> date.fromisoformat('2020W011xx') datetime.date(2019, 12, 30) >>> datetime.fromisoformat('2020010112') # the datetime parser rejects it ValueError: Invalid isoformat string: '2020010112' ``` `date.fromisoformat` admits inputs of length 7, 8 or 10. Both `parse_isoformat_date()` in `Modules/_datetimemodule.c` and `_parse_isoformat_date()` in `Lib/_pydatetime.py` read fixed-width fields from the start of the string, and neither checks that the whole string was consumed. A 10-character string without `-` at index 4 is therefore parsed as the 8-character basic date `YYYYMMDD` (or `YYYYWwwD`), and the trailing characters are ignored. Such a string is not an ISO 8601 date, and it is not one of the documented exceptions. Because the result is a plausible date, a truncated or mistyped input (such as a 10-digit `YYYYMMDDHH`) goes unnoticed. Checked on: - 3.11.15 with the C accelerator: the output above; - `Lib/_pydatetime.py` from `main` (7eada7c2c6), run under 3.11.15: same results for both strings; - `Modules/_datetimemodule.c` on `main`: read, not built. The code path is unchanged. Suggested fix: after the last field, require that the whole string has been consumed (`p - dtstr == len` in C, `len(dtstr) == pos` in Python). I have a draft patch with tests for both implementations and can open a PR if this is accepted. Found by differential testing `fromisoformat` against an independent ISO 8601 implementation. I found no existing report; the nearest is gh-152204, which covers other pure-Python-only inputs. ### CPython versions tested on: 3.11, CPython main branch ### Operating systems tested on: Windows ### Linked PRs * gh-158557

title: fs: heap buffer overflow in readFileSync(fd, "utf8") when a pipe returns short reads
excerpt: ### Version v26.10.0 (also present in v26.8.0 through v26.10.0 and v24.21.0; not present in v26.7.0 or v22.23.3) ### Platform ```text Linux archpc 7.2.4-arch1-2 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:22:31 +0000 x86_64 GNU/Linux Arch Linux, nodejs 26.10.0-1, glibc 2.44 ``` ### Subsystem fs ### What steps will reproduce the bug? ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # Producer: 24 short writes (~96 KiB, each read back as a short read), then one large write. node -e ' const chunk = "x".repeat(4000); let i = 0; const t = setInterval(() => { process.stdout.write(chunk); if (++i === 24) { clearInterval(t); process.stdout.write("y".repeat(400000)); } }, 5); ' | node -e 'console.log(require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8").length)' echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[1]}" ``` ### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition? 10 of 10 runs with the script above. The input must be a pipe (or FIFO, or `/dev/stdin` backed by one) that delivers more than 64 KiB in reads shorter than 8 KiB before the first full 8 KiB read. Regular files are not affected. The encoding does not matter: the input above is pure ASCII. Real-world trigger: `some-test-runner | node -e 'require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")...'`, where the producer writes in small chunks. It crashed at 7 of 60 runs with a ~420 KB input written in 4093-byte chunks. ### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior? Prints `496000` and exits 0, as v26.7.0 does and as `readFileSync(0).toString("utf8")` does on v26.10.0. ### What do you see instead? ```text malloc(): invalid size (unsorted) exit=134 ``` SIGABRT from glibc. Symbolized stack (from a real crash, via debuginfod.archlinux.org): ```text #6 malloc_printerr (str="malloc(): invalid size (unsorted)") at malloc.c:5093 #7 _int_malloc (av= , bytes=427486) at malloc.c:3683 #10 __GI___libc_realloc (oldmem=0x0, bytes=427486) at malloc.c:3198 #11 node::UncheckedRealloc (pointer=0x0, n= ) at ../../src/util-inl.h:267 #13 node::MaybeStackBuffer ::AllocateSufficientStorage (storage=213743) at ../../src/util-inl.h:544 #14 node::StringBytes::Encode (...) at ../../src/string_bytes.cc:659 #15 node::fs::ReadFileUtf8 (args=...) at ../../src/node_file.cc:3559 ``` The abort happens later than the corruption. The corruption itself is a heap buffer overflow in `ReadFileUtf8`. ### Additional information Cause, in `ReadFileUtf8` ([src/node_file.cc#L3511-L3523 at v26.10.0](https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/59da6b44a953cf9b45f2591ae80f569ce1ec9da5/src/node_file.cc#L3511-L3523)): - While `big == nullptr`, every short read (`r big_cap`, so `big_len == big_cap` never matches, and `big_cap - big_len` in the next `uv_buf_init` underflows. A possible fix: size the first allocation from what is already buffered, for example `big_cap = std::max(kMinChunk, result.size() + sizeof(buffer))`, and make the growth check `big_len >= big_cap`. Workaround: `fs.readFileSync(0).toString("utf8")` avoids the fast path.

title: Discussion: preserving TCP peer addresses at accept time
excerpt: I'd like to revisit a long-standing `net.Socket` behavior, following an investigation and proof of concept in libuv: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/5308 This is closely related to [nodejs/node#23858](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/23858), opened in 2018, where `socket.remoteAddress`, `remotePort`, and `remoteFamily` could already be `undefined` inside the server's connection handler. That discussion ended without a fix, but a maintainer comment also left room for reconsideration if a stronger technical case could be made. I've tried to approach this follow-up in that spirit: I traced the behavior through the Node.js and libuv history, examined the relevant Linux kernel semantics, built a libuv proof of concept that preserves the accept-time peer address, and benchmarked its connection-throughput cost. The findings point to an information-lifetime issue at the libuv layer. Preserving the accept-time address also has a different performance profile from restoring the old unconditional `getpeername()` call. ## What happens On Unix, libuv accepts incoming TCP connections without requesting the peer sockaddr from `accept()` / `accept4()`. When Node.js later needs the remote address, libuv calls `getpeername()` on the accepted socket. Normally that works. However, a connection can complete successfully and then be reset before the application processes it. The distinction between obtaining the peer address as part of `accept()` and querying it later with `getpeername()` is part of the original BSD sockets API design, introduced with 4.2BSD in 1983; it is not specific to Linux. The Linux reproducer demonstrates why this distinction matters: `accept()` can still return the peer address even when a subsequent `getpeername()` fails with `ENOTCONN`. Once the accept-time sockaddr has been discarded, the later query cannot recover it. A reproducer in the libuv issue demonstrates this using a normal TCP `connect()` followed by an abortive close with `SO_LINGER`. In one 100,000-connection run using Node.js v26.10.0 / libuv v1.52.1: ```text upstream: Address: 3,268 Undefined: 96,732 patched: Address: 100,000 Undefined: 0 ``` The exact percentage is timing-dependent. The relevant observation is that the connections completed and were accepted, but their peer addresses could become unavailable before the later query. Preserving the sockaddr returned at accept time eliminated that failure mode in this test. ## Historical context I documented the relevant Node.js and libuv history here: https://github.com/bobnil/libuv-accept-peer-address-poc/blob/main/HISTORICAL_CONTEXT.md Before the libuv backend, Node's networking code retained the peer address returned by the accept operation. The first public Node.js/libuv backend retained the accepted fd but did not propagate the accept-time peer address with it. The address was subsequently obtained through a separate `getpeername()` query. Node initially performed that query eagerly. In 2011, it was made lazy, a

title: Unexpected server incoming requests queue after Node.js 20 version (possible performance regression)
excerpt: ### Version v22.14.0 ### Platform ```text Darwin macbook-JPF9H46PN7 23.5.0 Darwin Kernel Version 23.5.0: Wed May 1 20:12:58 PDT 2024; root:xnu-10063.121.3~5/RELEASE_ARM64_T6000 arm64 ``` ### Subsystem http ### What steps will reproduce the bug? Repository with reproduction - https://github.com/SuperOleg39/node-js-perf-problem-reproduction About repo: `server.js` - a http server with: - `/`, `/test/` and `/unknown/` endpoinds with cpu-heavy work emulation - 5 parallel request processing limit for this endpoints for event loop overload protection - `/readyz` health check endpoint - `/metrics` metrics endpoint - `/`, `/test/` and `/unknown/` handlers wrapped in `setImmediate` to split heavy tasks by different event loop tasks `server.test.js` - performance test case for this server: - `autocannon` make a 1000 concurrent requests for 1 minute to server endpoints `/`, `/test/` and `/unknown/` - in parallel run 5 seconds interval with request to `/readyz` For reproduction, need to run `server.js` with different node.js versions, and run `server.test.js` for every try (more in repository README.md) ### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition? It works correctly at 16, 18 and 19 Node.js versions, but not works at 20 and 22 versions. ### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior? Event loop lag is small, incoming health check requests is processed fast, 10s ### Additional information Hello! We have a integration test for custom requests limiter, working on the principle of awesome [under-pressure](https://github.com/fastify/under-pressure) library - in summary with this requests limiter Node.js application can be responsive even under high load. This test emulates a high load and endpoints with CPU-heavy work, and expects that fast requests to health checks or metrics will be processed almost immediately. After update Node.js to v20 in our CI, we saw a failed test with very slow healthcheck responses. I spend a few days to debug, and main results is: - event loop is not overloaded, lag is less than 500ms (okay for this test) - in CPU profile I can see microtasks between `setImmediate` calls - but incoming `/readyz` requests start to be processed after 10-20 seconds - problem somewere in core modules, because this lag starts from the request handler - `http.createServer(handler)` - and also deeper, event before internal `server.emit('request')` call. - if we split healthchecks and metrics endpoints to different http server in the same Node.js process, it respond fast in all Node.js versions - one more confirmation that there is some queue at the level of a particular http server

title: Prevent native Error class hi-jacking in FS errors
excerpt: ### Version v16.9.0 ### Platform Linux vagrant-docker 4.19.0-6-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 4.19.67-2+deb10u2 (2019-11-11) x86_64 GNU/Linux ### Subsystem fs ### What steps will reproduce the bug? In the current state of the `promises` section of the native `fs` module, when an error occurs, the native type `Error` is hi-jacked and a `code` property is being added to the error object. This can easily be reproduced with the following code: ```javascript import { promises as FileSystem } from "fs"; try { FileSystem.stat("/a/path/leading/to/nothing"); } catch (error) { console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(error); // Will display the native class "Error" console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors(error); // Will display the added code property that isn't native to Error. } ``` ### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition? No required conditions outside of the use of the `fs` native module. ### What is the expected behavior? This isn't a bug per-se but is a bad practice. A custom error of type `FileSystemError` should be thrown instead of hi-jacking the Error class to dynamically add a property to the object. This behavior leads to problematic linting and testing with super-sets such as TypeScript or Eslint.
